source: Schwartz and Martin (2004) Inventing to prepare for future learning, Experiment 1
finding: Ninth graders who invented methods before a lecture did better on a transfer problem only when the test itself held a worked-example resource (double-transfer design). Without the resource, invention and tell-and-practice looked the same.
numbers: Six intact classes, 95 students with pre and post. Posttest acceptable solutions on the standardized-score problem: invention no resource 30.4% (n=23), invention with resource 60.8% (n=23), tell-and-practice no resource 32.0% (n=25), with resource 29.2% (n=24). Correct quantitative: 8.7, 30.4, 4.0, 12.5%. Three-way interaction F(1,91)=4.9. 91.7% followed the worked example.
quote: students in the invention and tell-and-practice conditions performed about the same when they did not receive the resource
limits: Classes, not students, were assigned. At pretest 17% scored 1 or 2 on the target. The authors say the benefit was topic specific. One design team and one lab.
agent_relevance: The benefit of attempt-first showed only when a later resource could be used. For an agent: lessons memory pays off when a worked solution is in view, not as a blind gain. Test with and without a worked-solution step.

source: Schwartz and Martin (2004) Inventing to prepare for future learning, Experiment 2 (four teachers)
finding: Experiment 2 had four classroom teachers run the lessons. The pattern repeated with a smaller gain.
numbers: Posttest acceptable solutions: invention no resource 18.2% (n=20), invention with resource 45.8% (n=23), tell-and-practice no resource 26.6% (n=28), with resource 21.9% (n=31). Correct quantitative 9.1, 33.3, 13.3, 15.6%. Three-way interaction F(1,98)=4.4. Bivariate-variance problem rose from 7.1% to 21.4%; 33.8% showed negative transfer of the mean deviation.
limits: Same authors; researchers were present and joined class discussion about 25% of the time. One teacher who favoured direct instruction was uncomfortable in early cycles. The with-resource invention score fell from 60.8 to 45.8.
agent_relevance: The effect shrank when other teachers ran it, a first sign that it depends on implementation. Vary the lessons prompt in an agent run.

source: Schwartz and Martin (2004), delayed posttest and college benchmark
finding: A random subset of 30 ninth graders was tested again one year later. Many could still compute the mean deviation. There was no control group at the delayed test.
numbers: Mean deviation computed correctly: 5% pretest, 86% posttest, 57% at one year (n=30). College students after a semester of statistics: none computed a reasonable answer. Bivariate-variance problem: 10.6% pretest, 34% posttest, vs 12% of college students.
limits: Retention is for the whole invention curriculum, with no tell-and-practice delayed comparison. It is not a retention effect of PF. Gap 10 stays open.
agent_relevance: Long-delay evidence for PF is thinner than the series assumed. For an agent, retention across sessions needs its own test.

source: Kapur, Saba and Roll (2023) Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure (npj Science of Learning)
finding: The number of representations and solution methods (RSMs) a group generated predicted posttest score. Prior math achievement mostly did not. Two schools with very different prior achievement made similar numbers of RSMs. This is an association inside PF, not a manipulation.
numbers: Two quasi-experimental studies in 2 Singapore schools: 112 seventh graders (ratios) and 105 eighth graders (variance). ANCOVA with school, PSLE math grade, pretest and RSM count. Ratios: RSMs F(1,107)=62.589, p<0.001; PSLE math F(1,107)=4.436, p=0.032; pretest p=0.102; school p=0.471. Variance: RSMs F(1,100)=105.518, p<0.001; PSLE math F=0.001, p=0.980. School gap in PSLE math d=2.12 (grade 7) and 1.23 (grade 8).
limits: RSM count was not manipulated. Groups worked together but PSLE was individual, so weak members were credited with group RSMs (authors' limitation). Authors cite two earlier studies with the same materials that found no link between RSMs and conceptual posttest. Same lab as the originator.
agent_relevance: Correlate, not proven cause. To use it in an agent, force diversity as an intervention and compare with unforced runs.

source: Braas, Hartmann, Hoogerheide, Rummel and van Gog (2025) When is observing failure productive? Solution diversity in vicarious failure (Instructional Science)
finding: Randomised test in which the diversity of attempts was manipulated by supplying them. Students who watched five attempts covering all four canonical components (VF-high) beat those who watched attempts covering two (VF-low) and beat direct instruction. VF-high matched PF. The PF versus DI effect did not replicate.
numbers: N=152 secondary students, random assignment to PF (n=37), VF-high (n=39), VF-low (n=34), DI (n=36). Conceptual posttest F(3,140)=3.078, p=.030, partial eta2=.062. Means: PF 1.47, VF-high 1.84, VF-low 1.25, DI 1.05. VF-high vs VF-low d=0.644 (p=.014); VF-high vs DI d=0.648 (p=.010); VF-high vs PF d=0.292 (p=.193, ns); PF vs DI d=0.294 (p=.170, ns). Procedural F(3,148)=1.987, p=.118.
quote: students' activation of prior knowledge is more critical than whether they experience failure first hand
limits: Math, individual work, video modelling. Conceptual scores are low. Supplied diversity is a causal manipulation, but of watched attempts, not own attempts.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence on gaps 4 and 5. Diversity is causal when supplied, and a supplied failed attempt can equal a self-generated one. For an agent: seeded diverse failed attempts may stand in for its own, if they cover the needed components.

source: Braas et al. (2025), PF arm detail and comparison with earlier PF studies
finding: In the PF arm, the quality of attempts, counted as canonical components used, tracked outcome. Attempt count was lower than in the originator lab's classes. The paper lists mean solutions per student in earlier studies.
numbers: PF students generated M=3.63 solutions, with 1.22 canonical components each. Components vs conceptual score r=.418, p=.009; full range of components r=.211, p=.204. Earlier PF means quoted by the authors: Kapur and Bielaczyc 2012 6.03; Kapur 2014b 6.08; Kapur 2014a 6.15; Loibl 2014b 5.10 and 4.13; Hartmann 2020 4.54; Hartmann 2021 2.95; Hartmann 2023 3.13; Loibl 2020 2.78.
limits: Secondhand for Kapur 2012 and 2014 (cited, not opened). The pattern of 6+ solutions in the originator lab vs 3-4 elsewhere was not tested. Authors say individuals made as many solutions as groups, so collaboration does not explain it.
agent_relevance: Gives trace metrics: attempts per item and canonical-component coverage. Log both in agent attempt traces.

source: Nachtigall, Serova and Rummel (2020) When failure fails to be productive (Instructional Science)
finding: Two quasi-experiments in German 10th-grade social science research methods. Study 1: PF did worse than DI. Study 2: no difference, moderate evidence for the null. PF groups did generate several different solution ideas, so a low attempt count does not explain Study 1.
numbers: Study 1 N=212 (eight schools): transfer scale F(1,210)=31.11, partial eta2=.13, DI higher; total outcome F(1,209)=27.46, partial eta2=.12, DI higher. PF groups (n=44) averaged 3.93 solution ideas (SD 1.43); the best idea used 5.07 of 8 canonical principles; no group solved it canonically. Study 2 N=152 (seven classes): condition F(1,148)=0.32, p=.57, partial eta2=.002; Bayesian ANOVA BF10=0.23.
limits: Not STEM; no pretest (to avoid priming); class-level assignment. Study 1 went the wrong way, which is stronger than a null.
agent_relevance: Attempt count did not cause this failure. It weakens one explanation in K05. Log coverage and typical-error match, not only count.

source: Nachtigall et al. (2020), perceived competence in PF and its link to learning
finding: PF students felt more competent after the attempt phase than DI students, then their confidence dropped after instruction. A larger drop went with lower learning. The authors read this as lack of awareness of limits before instruction.
numbers: Study 1: PF perceived competence 3.53 (SD 0.63) after phase 1 and 3.02 (SD 0.90) after phase 2; time effect F(1,120)=23.12, p<.001, partial eta2=.21. Drop vs learning outcome r=-0.36, p<.001. Study 2: higher competence in PF after phase 1, F(1,150)=5.33, p=.02, partial eta2=.03.
limits: Self-report in students; the drop-vs-learning link is a post hoc correlation. In earlier math work (Loibl and Rummel 2015) PF students' competence rose between phases.
agent_relevance: A weak human hint on gap 9: attempt-first can leave inflated confidence until the lesson. In an agent, log confidence before and after the lesson step against accuracy. No LLM measurement was found.

source: Loibl and Leuders (2024) Can failure be made productive also in Bayesian reasoning? A conceptual replication (Instructional Science)
finding: Conceptual replication of Loibl and Rummel (2014a) with Bayesian reasoning. No effect of problem-solving-first and no effect of building the instruction on typical student solutions. Most students made one attempt.
numbers: N=75 in a 2x2 (PS-I vs I-PS; instruction with vs without typical student solutions). Order effect tests not significant (for example F(1,71)=0.04, p=.84). 31 of 38 PS-first students gave exactly one solution attempt and applied it to all three tasks.
limits: About 19 per cell. Authors name two mechanisms: students only activated prior probability knowledge without exploring, and the lesson's typical solutions did not match what students produced.
agent_relevance: Fits a low-coverage explanation here (one attempt) where Nachtigall does not. The failures share no single feature: few attempts (Loibl and Leuders), wrong domain (Nachtigall), low diversity (Braas). Log attempts and lesson match in agent traces.

source: Sinha and Kapur (2021) When problem solving followed by instruction works (Review of Educational Research), full abstract via Crossref
finding: The abstract confirms the pooled effect and gives the moderators. Younger children (grades 2 to 5) and domain-general skills favoured instruction-first. Quasi-experimental nature, grade level and time span contributed to the effect. The bias-adjusted g=0.87 is the authors' own estimate.
numbers: 53 studies, 166 comparisons. Hedges g=0.36 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.51). High-fidelity PF: g from 0.37 to 0.58. After publication-bias adjustment g=0.87. Crossref lists 78 references; only 8 mention Kapur in the reference string, but the list holds cited works, not the included-study table.
limits: Full text returned HTTP 403 (Sage), and ResearchGate and Semantic Scholar were blocked. The study table, lab share and per-domain values were NOT read. Gap 1 stays open for those. Larger effects in quasi-experiments flag a weakness in the evidence.
agent_relevance: Do not treat 0.87 as a target. The moderators say the sign flips for novices and general skills. Report per-type results in our test.

source: Kapur, Hattie, Grossman and Sinha (2022) Fail, Flip, Fix, and Feed (Frontiers in Education)
finding: The originator group's later review restates Sinha and Kapur (2021). Its own flipped-learning meta-analysis does not directly compare problem-first with instruction-first, and the pre-class problem-set comparison is not significant.
numbers: Own meta-analysis: 173 articles, 192 samples, 532 effect sizes, N=43,278, g=0.37 (CI 0.32 to 0.41); 90% university students. Problem sets: flipped g=0.40 (n=410) vs control 0.30 (n=122), difference 0.10, p=0.201. Pre-class assignments g=0.18 (10 studies). Restates PS-I g=0.36, high fidelity 0.37 to 0.58, adjusted 0.87.
limits: First 100,000 of 183,767 characters read. Authors include the PF originator, so the PS-I numbers are not independent of K01.
agent_relevance: Same source as Sinha and Kapur for counting. The flipped-class result is weaker than the headline PF claims suggest.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) In-context principle learning from mistakes (LEAP)
finding: The nearest published test of attempt-first lessons for a model. The model first answers the few-shot examples with sampled chain of thought, is then shown the ground-truth answer to explain each error, and uses the distilled principles on new questions. Gains are small and uneven. It compares with few-shot CoT, not with an instruction-first order.
numbers: Few-shot CoT vs LEAP high-level (low-level): DROP GPT-4 72.05 to 78.60 (79.55); HotpotQA GPT-4 36.35 to 39.65; DROP GPT-4-turbo 83.40 to 80.00; HotpotQA Gemini Pro 28.25 to 25.50 (23.70). GSM8K GPT-3.5 76.4 to 76.6 (77.4); GPT-4 93.6 to 93.8 (94.2); Claude-2 84.3 to 83.8 (82.7). MATH GPT-4 63.5 to 64.0 (64.5); Gemini Pro 31.1 to 30.3 (29.7). In BBH one LEAP variant beat the baseline in 37 of 42 task-model pairs.
limits: The lessons step uses the ground-truth answer (oracle). Not token matched. No intervals and apparently single runs per cell.
agent_relevance: Closest to gaps 2 and 7 but it tests 'learn from own mistakes with the right answer' and not 'attempt first versus lesson first'. Effects of 0 to 8 points mean our test needs many items.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) LEAP, open-source failure
finding: With Llama-2-chat-70B as the model, LEAP made results worse, even when GPT-4 wrote the principles. The model produced sensible principles but did not follow them.
numbers: Llama-2-chat-70B GSM8K few-shot CoT 52.5; LEAP low-level 50.6 (own critic) and 49.8 (GPT-4 critic); high-level 47.0 and 51.0. MATH baseline 16.2; LEAP low-level 13.8 and 12.9; high-level 14.2 and 13.8.
limits: Preliminary experiments in the authors' words; one older open model.
agent_relevance: A lesson from a stronger source (a supplied lesson, gap 5) did not help a model that could not use it. Test our agent per model.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion, verifier-quality results
finding: When the success signal is self-written tests, lessons help only if the tests are reliable. Without tests, reflection hurt. With a noisy test suite on MBPP Python, Reflexion fell below the baseline.
numbers: HumanEval Python 0.80 to 0.91, false-positive rate 0.01 (text: 1.4%). MBPP Python 0.80 to 0.77, false-positive rate 0.16 (text: 16.3%). HumanEval Rust hard-50 (GPT-4): base 0.60; no test generation 0.52; tests but no reflection 0.60; both 0.68. HotPotQA: the CoT agent given ground-truth context was still wrong on 39% of questions, and Reflexion without ground truth improved accuracy by 14%.
limits: The Rust ablation has 50 problems. Test noise is the difference the authors point to between the Python sets; others are possible.
agent_relevance: Direct data for gap 3: reliable check +11 points (HumanEval), noisy check -3 points (MBPP), no check -8 points (Rust ablation) relative to baseline. Verifier quality gates the lessons step.

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han and Zhang (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey
finding: Survey of self-correction. No prior work shows successful self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback in general tasks. It works with reliable external feedback, or in tasks where checking is much easier than solving.
numbers: Three headline claims: (1) no prior work shows reliable in-context self-correction except in tasks exceptionally suited to it; (2) it works with reliable external feedback; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Bottleneck named as feedback generation.
limits: Survey; no pooled numbers. The authors urge analysis of the quality of the feedback itself.
agent_relevance: Supports K17 and gap 3: do not trust lessons from an unverified own attempt. Design rule: score the verifier before the lesson.

source: An, Ma, Lin, Zheng, Lou and Chen (2024) Learning from mistakes makes LLM better reasoner (LeMa)
finding: Fine-tuning on other models' failed solutions, each corrected by GPT-4 with an explanation, improved math reasoning over chain-of-thought-only fine-tuning. Dropping the corrected solution or the explanation hurt; dropping the marked mistake step hurt less. GPT-4 corrected its own mistakes far less often than others' mistakes.
numbers: GPT-4 corrected 217 of 2,696 own wrong MATH paths = 8.0%; it corrected LLaMA-2-70B mistakes at 37.5% and GPT-3.5-Turbo mistakes at 26.9%. As corrector, GPT-3.5-Turbo gave poor quality in nearly half of 20 sampled corrections.
limits: Fine-tuning, not prompting. Self vs other rates are confounded with question difficulty (authors' own caveat).
agent_relevance: Weak evidence on gap 5: supplied failures plus a correct explanation are useful for training. The correct solution and explanation matter more than whose failure it was.

source: Chung, Du and Fu (2025) Learning from failures in multi-attempt reinforcement learning
finding: Training a small model on a multi-attempt task, with feedback after each wrong answer, improved accuracy when more attempts were allowed. A single-turn-trained model hardly improved. This is training with an oracle, not a scaffold.
numbers: Qwen 2.5 Math 1.5B, five math benchmarks averaged. Multi-attempt trained: 45.6% with 1 attempt to 52.5% with 2 attempts. Single-turn trained: 42.3% to 43.2%. Reward +1 if correct in any attempt, -0.5 if wrong but right format, -1 otherwise.
limits: The feedback is a right-or-wrong oracle. More attempts spend more tokens, so it is not equal-token. RL training, not a prompt.
agent_relevance: Does not answer gap 2 (equal tokens). Shows retries need a clean wrong/right signal to pay off.

source: Kapur (2012) Productive failure in learning the concept of variance (Instructional Science), abstract only
finding: Only the abstract was readable. Ninth graders generated many formulations for variance but not the canonical one, then outperformed direct-instruction students on conceptual understanding and transfer without losing procedural fluency.
numbers: No effect sizes available: the full text is paywalled. Braas et al. (d06) quote the PF arm of Kapur and Bielaczyc 2012 as 6.03 solutions per student.
limits: Abstract only. The Kapur 2014 pages (Cognitive Science, JLS) returned 403. Gap 6 stays open for Kapur 2012 and 2014.
agent_relevance: Cannot size any effect from this. Keep K03 as single-source.
